anchor.quote: Here $b$ is the number of bits in each radix digit, so the radix is $2^b$.
The integers $c_0, c_1, \dots$ (lowest position first) represent the product as $\sum_k c_k\, 2^{bk}$.

anchor.note: Summation index of the finite sum $\sum_k$ in standard sigma notation, used with the series and geometric sums the reader already knows; the page's phrase "lowest position first" indicates that k runs over positions. The earlier-page bindings of k (output index, denominator exponent) are different roles and are not used here.

gaps.term: Rounding of Gaussian dyadic values to integers
gaps.quote: to the nearest integers, which is exact arithmetic on power-of-two denominators.
gaps.note: This is cited, and the page does not say what it states or why it applies. It does not say how rounding a Gaussian dyadic value (a complex number with dyadic real and imaginary parts) to nearest integers is done, for example componentwise on the real and imaginary parts, and it does not say why this is exact. It also conflicts with the earlier sentence that the computed values are real, so the reader cannot tell how the complex values become the real coefficients that are rounded.

gaps.quote: Because every coefficient is recovered exactly, the carried digits are the exact binary product.
gaps.note: The carry rule is stated for each position, but the page never says how many positions are processed or what happens to a carry left over after the highest coefficient. The example ends with a zero carry, but the page does not say that the carry is always zero at the end, so the reader cannot check that the carried digits give the whole product.
